title: Shape morphing through UI states
prompt_text: <inputs> Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use). </inputs> <direction> Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops. Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template. </direction> <structure> 120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat. Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button. </structure> <build> 1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames. 2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time. 3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob. 4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was. 5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak. 6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps. 7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read. </build> <gotchas> Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters. </gotchas> <start> Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code. </start>

title: Photo print app launch film
prompt_text: <inputs> Ask me for: a one-word brand name for the wordmark (a verb works best), 9 to 12 high-res photos, a royalty-free song around 120 BPM with a drop and a quiet breakdown (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and a free stock clip of a plain wall with moving plant shadows (Pexels). </inputs> <direction> An Apple-keynote launch film, 2D only, one continuous take. Every scene is made out of the previous one: nothing fades, blurs or cuts. Objects change shape instead: text rises out of a mask line, icons pop from zero on a spring, bars draw across, pages push, and a black shape floods the whole frame and contracts into the next scene. Warm off-white canvas, black UI, iOS 26 liquid glass over the photos. Archivo (wdth 125, weight 800) for the wordmark, Geist for UI. A cursor drives every change with real clicks, drags and long-presses. The camera zooms screen-studio style so each moment fills the square, and the cursor scales with it. Banned: crossfades, blur-ins, brightness "developing", 3D flips, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, anything that looks like a template. </direction> <structure> 120 BPM, 54 beats, something happens on every beat. Open: the wordmark squeezes into its own period like an accordion, the dot grows into a black pill, a label rises inside it. Click: six iris blades close over the label and snap open onto a photo. The circle becomes a square, shrinks, the grid unfolds from behind it like a paper map (center, plus, corners), reflows into a bento, and a click zooms into one tile, landing exactly on the drop. Glass: a glass word pops in letter by letter, melts into a droplet that stretches into a glass toolbar. The adjust icon turns it into a slider. Dragging relights the photo from day to golden hour (two aligned shots), and the knob turns into a glass lens while held. It lifts into a glass orb, the next photo opens inside it as a circle, and the orb expands into a lock screen: glass clock digits, date, and a home bar that stretches into a glass music player. Stage: the lock screen pulls back into a phone (the bezel grows out of the screen edge). The Dynamic Island stretches like liquid, pinches off, flies over and grows into a Mac window that rolls up like a blind. Long-press the wallpaper, drag it onto a Safari tab, the page pushes in, drop it and it becomes the hero of a landing page. Scroll: the hero morphs into a framed print on a product card, with the mat and molding growing out of the photo's edge. Pick a frame color (it paints across) and a size, then the nav button flies down into "Order print". Order: one black shape keeps morphing: Ordered ✓ → Printing % → On its way (a van on a route) → Delivered ✓. Wall: the delivered circle floods the frame edge to edge, holds black for a beat, and contracts into the framed print hanging on the real wall footage. The same iris opens onto the print, closes again, the frame floods the screen and contracts into the pill → the dot → the letters spring back out, landing on the beat return. Last frame = first frame. </structure> <build> 1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside an async seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state between frames. 2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value with many targets is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time. 3. Liquid glass: each glass element holds its own clone of the scene behind it, filtered with an SVG feImage displacement map (a rounded-rect distance field) through three feDisplacementMaps at slightly different scales for chromatic edges, plus a rim light. Glass letters: a canvas distance field per glyph gives the map, mask and highlights. 4. Goo: blur + alpha threshold, then composite the source atop it so the glass stays sharp inside. 5. Iris: 6 blades around a hexagonal aperture. Each blade is its two vertices, both edge extensions and the SHORT arc between them. 6. Wordmark squeeze: every letter moves toward the dot by the same factor and its drawn width follows (narrow the wdth axis, scale the rest), so the letters stay touching. 7. Footage: re-encode all-intra (ffmpeg -g 1), load it as a blob URL, await 'seeked' before drawing each frame. 8. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event (Mixkit), never synthesized, each placed by its measured peak. The song starts on a downbeat: the zoom lands on the drop, the wall sits in the breakdown, the wordmark returns with the beat. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS. 9. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame blended with ffmpeg tmix, 60fps. Check one frame per beat, then scan for single-frame pops (frame-difference spikes 3x their neighbours). </build> <gotchas> backdrop-filter: url() misreads displacement maps in Chromium, so clone the scene instead. A flood must overscale past the corners and take about 0.3s, or half the screen changes in one frame. A child with visibility: visible shows through a hidden parent, so use inherit. Text that swaps inside a morphing shape needs its own mask. python http.server can't range-seek video, so use the blob URL. </gotchas> <start> Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 4 stills (open, glass, stage, wall) before you write the full film. </start>

title: Landing page 3D scroll
prompt_text: <inputs> Ask me for: my landing page link, my brand name and logo mark, a two-part closing line (a statement, then a short italic tail), and a 15 second track (optional). </inputs> <direction> A 14.5 second 3D fly-over of my landing page, 1440x1152 at 60fps. The page lies flat on a bright studio floor (#f9fbfb in the middle, #f2f3f6 in the corners) with a soft wide shadow around it and 24px rounded corners. One continuous camera, never a cut: it starts low over the hero and glides backwards down the page at one steady speed while looking up it, rises straight overhead to show the whole page as one strip, dives into the hero and lands it as a card under a two-line title. Focus is razor thin in front of the subject and almost none behind it, so everything near the lens melts. Cards float a little above the page with soft shadows; photos, chips and the testimonial lift off and stand up toward the lens as the camera passes them. Four small tiles of my logo lift off beside the hero button and stay with the film until the end card. The title is Geist 500, the italic tail Instrument Serif. Banned: cuts, crossfades, stops or surges in the glide, the camera turning or swinging sideways, zooming in and back out, glows, any text laid over the page before the end card. </direction> <structure> 14.5 seconds: flight 0-8.2s, rise 7.75-9.25s, overhead 9.25-9.47s, dive 9.47-9.97s, title card 9.97-14.5s. The camera 56° off straight-down and 1360px from the point it looks at, centred on the top half of the hero, the phone or product mockup sharp, four 32px logo tiles beside the button → 0-0.6: the glide eases in from rest → 0.1-1.35: the tiles lift, grow to 140-200px and hang just outside the page's top corners while the hero's chips rise to 60-80px and stand up 30° → 1.25-1.6: the glide doubles to cruising speed as the hero falls behind → 1.6: the second section's title passes the centre of the frame, its photos blurred near the lens → 1.35-2.7: that section's main photos lift to 100-130px and stand up 46°, two of its chips fly up to about 200px, stand up 54° and pass the left and right edges at 2.5 → 1.2-2.4: the tiles trail the camera 300px down the page, then drift out of the top → 3.0-7.3: every following section passes through at the same steady speed, each one sharp as it crosses the middle of the frame and soft below it; a logo tile drifts past the left edge close and blurred at 5.4 → 5.45-6.3: the testimonial card rises from 22 to 112px, stands up 30° and shows a 34px white edge → 7.3-8.2: the glide eases off as the footer arrives, the footer title sharp at 8.0 → 7.75-9.25: the rise, zooming out at an even rate while the tilt flattens (8.15-8.95) and the page's bottom edge settles 42px above the frame bottom → 9.25-9.47: the whole page as one centred strip, creeping 3.5% closer → 9.47-9.97: the dive, the page's top edge pinned to the frame top while it grows, everything below the hero fading out, then the top drops to y 283 so the hero lands as a 1018px wide card with 38px corners and a soft shadow; two logo tiles sit on its top corners, one crisp at the right edge, two huge soft blurs drift in at the bottom corners → 10.02: a white badge pill (logo + brand, 21px) fades in at y 44 → 10.12: line 1 at 74px, one word every 0.06s → 10.36: the italic tail at 82px in grey #8b8b92, one word every 0.05s, each word rising 16px out of a 12px blur in 0.34s → 10.6-14.5: hold, the card creeping 2% closer, the tiles drifting a few px. </structure> <build> 1. Open my link in headless Chromium (Playwright) at 1440px wide, device scale 2, and scroll to the bottom once so lazy images and scroll animations finish. Mark the pieces that lift (cards, phone or product mockups, chips, feature photos, the testimonial, the hero button) with data-layer. Screenshot the full page with them hidden, then each piece alone on a transparent background with 28px padding, and save every piece's page position to a JSON. 2. One WebGL2 film page, 1440x1152, every frame computed from time inside seek(t): no timers, no CSS transitions. The page is a textured quad on the floor and each piece its own quad at its height, drawn lowest first with no depth buffer. Use mipmaps and 16x anisotropic filtering or the far text shimmers. 3. Drive the camera from one speed curve, never from a position key every half second. Focal length 1880px, 56° tilt, distance easing out from 1360 to 1700px and never back in, no turning. Speed down the page as a share of cruise (cruise is about 770 page px/s): 0 at 0s, 0.5 by 0.6s, held at 0.5 to 1.25s, 1.0 by 1.6s, held between 0.94 and 1.1 to 7.3s, then easing to 0.12 by 8.3s. Integrate it into the page position. 4. Depth of field per pixel: blur radius = 75 x (focus - depth) / depth in front of the focus and 6 x (depth - focus) / depth behind it, capped at 120px, 40 taps on a golden-angle disc, each tap read from a mip level matched to the blur. Keep the focus on whatever crosses the middle of the frame. 5. A lifted piece stands up by turning about its own middle, top edge rising toward the lens. Each casts a shadow on whatever is under it: the same picture in flat #1a2133, offset (0.10z, 4 + 0.36z), blurred 7 + 0.5z, 26% opacity. 6. Rise: zoom out in log scale with a smooth trapezoid speed (speeding up 7.75-8.35s, even 8.35-8.95s, slowing to a stop at 9.25s) and hand the glide over to a camera that holds the page's bottom edge at that 42px line from 8.3 to 8.65s. Dive: log scale on a quadratic ease in-out, then solve the look-at point from the pinned edge. A rounded-rect mask morphs from the full page to the hero, 24px to 38px corners. 7. Render with Playwright on the real GPU (--use-angle=d3d11 --enable-gpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist): 60fps, 16 subframes across 0.7 of a frame for motion blur, H.264 MP4. The track's hit goes on 9.97s, whooshes on 8.66 and 9.80. </build> <gotchas> If you can't run code on my computer, tell me straight away that you can only make a live preview here and that the MP4 needs Claude Code. Phones or cards that fade out with transparency show whatever is behind them, so fade them into the haze colour first and only cut to transparent at the very end. Keep most lifts tiny (20-40px) and lock the page before timing anything, because any change in a section's height shifts everything after it. Before the final render, measure a quick 30fps preview with optical flow: the speed down the page must never dip and the zoom must never turn into a zoom-in during the flight. </gotchas> <start> Ask me for the inputs, capture my page, then show me stills at 0, 1.6, 2.5, 5, 6.5, 9.3 and 11 seconds before you render. </start>

prompt_text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product, the exact request a user types into it, 6 to 8 photos for the result cards, a royalty-free song around 130 BPM with a clear drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and my brand mark for the end card. If I skip anything, use the defaults: the food-ordering story below, food photos from Pexels (fire noodles, birria tacos, hot chicken, buffalo wings, smash burger, spicy ramen), and Mixkit "Cat Walk".
</inputs>

<direction>
A 15-second product launch film, 1920x1080 at 60fps. 2D only, one continuous take. No fades, blurs or cuts: each scene grows from the last. Text rises from a mask line, buttons expand into pages, and color floods from one object before shrinking into another. Give the camera one eased move per scene, and never zoom in and out consecutively.

Look: warm white canvas (#f5f5f2), black UI (#0e0e10), lime accent (#cdf24f), orange (#ff6a2a), and a blue send button (#2f6bff). Add an Apple Intelligence-style iridescent glow around the input: a blurred conic gradient rotating through pink, orange, lime, cyan and violet. Use real food photography on dark cards, Geist for UI and a serif for the product name on the end card.

Banned: crossfades, blur-ins, 3D, particles, camera moves that reverse direction, holds longer than 1s, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
130 BPM, 32 beats (14.8s). Start the song 12 beats before its drop.

Beats 0-6, ask: push slowly into the glowing composer, about 3x zoom. Type the request over three fixed lines with a natural keystroke rhythm:
"I'm really hungry, I don't know
what I want but something
spicy, crispy and filling"

Beat 6, send: press the send button. A lime ripple spreads from it and transforms the message into a chat bubble. Pull back once to reveal the phone around it (428x900 screen, 11px black bezel, 9:41 status bar).

Beats 6-12, think: the send button grows into an orange wok, a half-disc with a thin handle. It tosses 6 colorful ingredients on beats 8, 9, 10 and 11 beneath the shimmering text "Finding something for you…".

Beat 12, the drop: a lime circle expands from the wok to fill the frame in about 0.35s. Dark food cards (330x440, radius 28, photo on top, name, one-line description, price and rating) burst in from the center. Slide the strip across three cards and land on "Fire Noodles", which lifts with a "Best match" pill.

Beats 16-21, chat: the lime contracts back into the user's bubble, carrying its words as the chosen card flies into its slot. "Found it. Fire Noodles from Wok & Fire, smoky, spicy and seriously filling." rises in, followed by "Want me to order it for you?" Then show two pills: "Order now" in black and "More options" outlined. The cursor clicks Order now → spinner → "✓ Ordered".

Beats 21-32, outro: the black button expands into the page, staying pill-shaped as it reaches the edges while the camera pushes into it. Its label grows to headline size, then slides away. Bring in "You were craving noodles." and "Now it's on the way." word by word (92px, white on black). A courier dot follows a route to a pin. The pin becomes the brand mark, and the wordmark wipes out from behind it, with "made with" above and the product name below.
</structure>

3. Use closed-form step-response springs for every pop and settle.
4. Make every handoff a shared element: the lime flood carries a copy of the bubble's words, and the button carries its label into the page.
5. Sound: use a downloaded Mixkit SFX for each event - typing, send pop, each toss, drop impact, card swoosh, click, success tone, page-fill whoosh and mark sparkle. Place each by its measured peak and loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps using 8 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix. Review every fast moment frame by frame and scan the full video for single-frame pops.
</build>

<gotchas>
Four subframes leave ghost copies on fast moves, so render 8 and slow the move down. The flood must reach the farthest corner and take about 0.35s, or it looks like a flash. Set z-index on every layer so the cards don't float above the flood. Keep the typed request on fixed lines so the camera never has to follow a wrapping cursor. Declare every variable before the first seek() call.

title: Morphing UI states loop
prompt_text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

prompt_text: Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.”  Treat this as an original miniature speech staged entirely through typography. Every line changes the architecture of the frame. The final declaration must stand on something the earlier words physically constructed.  Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.  ART DIRECTION Background #102820. Paper # F4E9D5. Structural accent # F2B544. A literary editorial world with the scale and confidence of a public monument. Use a high-contrast serif for the speech, a heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, and a restrained monospace for small timing marks. No distressed protest-poster clichés, megaphones, flags, crowds, microphones, or stock footage.  ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER “We were told to wait.” “So we learned the weight of waiting.” “Then one voice made room.” “Then another.” “Now the floor belongs to us.”  Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.  CENTRAL VISUAL RULE Words have assigned architectural roles. WAIT is a lintel. WAITING is a suspended load. VOICE is a support. ROOM is an opening. FLOOR is a platform. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms, not from separate illustrations placed behind text.  STORYBOARD 0.00–3.00 “We were told to wait.” The sentence occupies a narrow horizontal opening beneath a massive WAIT. The opening slowly compresses while the sentence remains readable. The pressure comes from the layout, not camera shake.  3.00–6.50 “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal the sentence in spoken phrase groups. WAITING lowers on two fine vertical rules. Those rules become suspension cables. A baseline bends under the visual load using a controlled vector deformation.  6.50–10.00 “Then one voice made room.” VOICE enters vertically and rotates into a structural support. It lifts one end of the baseline. The counter of the O in ROOM becomes an aperture. The next composition is revealed through that aperture.  10.00–12.50 “Then another.” A second support arrives. The tilted structure levels. This is the first moment of perfect horizontal alignment in the film. Use a brief stillness to make the change feel earned.  12.50–16.00 “Now the floor belongs to us.” Earlier structural words assemble into a platform. The final sentence settles onto it. US receives emphasis through shared alignment and scale, never through a separate flashy effect.  16.00–18.00 Hold the complete declaration. A slight release of tension travels through the supporting rules. No new text. No restless decorative motion.  18.00–20.00 The camera tracks beneath the completed platform. Its underside fills the frame and becomes the opening WAIT lintel. Under full occlusion, return hidden elements to their initial positions. Reveal the exact opening composition.  CHOREOGRAPHY Do not force the speech onto a dance beat. Use a cue sheet based on phrases, pauses, and emphasis. Phrase reveals should follow reading order. Allow at least one 400ms moment of absolute stillness. Use critically damped motion for settling loads. Use controlled elastic deformation for the baseline only. Make the changes in available space carry the emotional progression.  TYPE IMPLEMENTATION Use actual glyph paths for structural words. Preserve counters and legibility during deformation. For transitions between unrelated words, use occlusion or matched structural edges; do not interpolate arbitrary path points. Keep the currently spoken phrase readable before it becomes architecture.  ENGINEERING Implement window. seek(t) as a deterministic scene renderer. No accumulated physics, autonomous CSS transitions, or changing random values. Use time-remapping curves and analytic transforms. Use a 20-second periodic timeline with render(0)=render(20). Provide fixed-step access at n/60 for 1200 export frames. Audio is optional and off by default; no browser speech synthesis or autoplay dependency.  QUALITY GATE Inspect eight representative frames. Check that the speech reads in the correct order. Check that structural transformations never destroy a line before the audience can read it. Check the final platform is visibly assembled from earlier elements. Return the complete HTML implementation.

title: Taxtello bookkeeping app film
prompt_text:
You are the senior motion designer, product designer and Remotion engineer for Taxtello.

Your task is to create a genuinely premium, Apple-level product film for Taxtello.

This is NOT a generic SaaS explainer.
This is NOT a feature walkthrough.
This is NOT a startup template animation.

I want a maximum 15-second brand/product showreel that makes Taxtello look like a mature, expensive, beautifully designed financial product.

Think:

Apple product launch film
× premium fintech
× editorial motion design
× restrained Stripe-like product presentation
× Taxtello's own visual identity

The desired reaction is:

“Wait, this is a German bookkeeping app?”

The film should feel expensive.

────────────────────────────────────
REPO / SOURCE OF TRUTH
────────────────────────────────────

First inspect the real repositories before designing anything.

Main product:
  /taxtello/main

Existing Remotion project:
  /taxtello/beta-motion

Important real brand sources:

  /taxtello/main/public/css/app/_00-tokens.css
  /taxtello/main/docs/design/TOKENS.md
  /taxtello/main/public/taxtello-wordmark.png
  /taxtello/main/public/icons.svg

Existing current product screenshots can be found under:

  /taxtello/main/artifacts/smoke-ui-smoke/

Prefer the newest valid screenshots/current source over stale artifacts.

There is already an existing 24-second Remotion hero animation in
/taxtello/beta-motion.

DO NOT replace it.
DO NOT regress it.
DO NOT force its current AI-connections storyline into this new film.

Create a new independent composition for this task, e.g.

  TaxtelloShowreel15

You may reuse good infrastructure, fonts, rendering utilities, motion primitives,
easing curves, asset loading and QA infrastructure from beta-motion where useful.

But creatively this should be a new film.

Before implementation, inspect the actual Taxtello UI and understand the product.

Do not invent functionality that does not exist.

────────────────────────────────────
REAL TAXTELLO VISUAL LANGUAGE
────────────────────────────────────

Use the real design system.

Core palette:

Background:
  #0c0f1a

Elevated surfaces:
  #111525
  #131722
  #1a2032

Primary brand gold:
  #e8b84b

Gold highlight:
  #f5d07a

Gold depth:
  #9b6d18

Primary text:
  #e8eaf2

Strong warm white:
  #f6f4eb

Secondary text:
  #8b93b5

Positive:
  #34d399

Negative/error only where semantically necessary:
  #f87171

Typography:
  Plus Jakarta Sans

Numbers / financial values where appropriate:
  JetBrains Mono

Use the actual Taxtello wordmark and/or Taxtello mark.
Do not redraw or approximate the logo.

Taxtello's gold should feel like a precious accent, not a yellow UI flood.

Think:
dark metal
warm gold
glass
ink
precision
quiet confidence

NOT:
cyberpunk
crypto
neon
gaming
generic AI purple
rainbow gradients

────────────────────────────────────
CORE CREATIVE RULES
────────────────────────────────────

Follow these rules ruthlessly:

1. ONE SHOT = ONE IDEA.

2. Every scene needs room to breathe.

3. The product UI is the hero.

4. Do not plaster explanatory copy everywhere.

5. Do not use hard cuts unless there is a deliberate reason.

6. Prefer object-driven transitions:
   a card becomes the next card,
   a chart line becomes a connector,
   a receipt becomes a booking,
   a number becomes another interface element,
   the camera moves through the product.

7. Use premium easing.
   No linear movement.

8. Motion should overlap naturally.
   Elements should not all start and stop at exactly the same frame.

9. Use depth sparingly:
   perspective,
   soft parallax,
   scale,
   foreground/background separation,
   controlled depth of field if achievable.

10. NO effect exists simply because it looks cool.

11. No particle spam.

12. No fake glassmorphism everywhere.

13. No excessive blur.

14. No pointless 3D spinning cards.

15. No constant zooming.

16. No 20 different animation styles.

17. No bouncing UI.

18. No giant marketing paragraph.

19. Do not imitate a particular Apple commercial shot-for-shot.
    Capture the philosophy and production quality instead.

The visual confidence should come from restraint.

────────────────────────────────────
FORMAT
────────────────────────────────────

Primary master:

1920 × 1080
60 fps
16:9
H.264
maximum duration: 15.0 seconds

Target runtime:
approximately 14.0–15.0 seconds.

It must work as a social-media product reveal even without sound.

If practical AFTER the master is finished, also create a deliberately recomposed
vertical/social variant.

Do not merely crop the desktop composition.

But the desktop master is the priority.

────────────────────────────────────
STORY / EMOTIONAL ARC
────────────────────────────────────

Do not make this a list of five features.

It should feel like one continuous thought:

CHAOS → CONTROL → CLARITY → TAXTELLO

The first 1.5 seconds must already look premium.

The first meaningful product moment should happen by ~2 seconds.

No five-second logo intro.

Possible narrative direction:

“Everything about your business, finally in one place.”

But SHOW this instead of explaining it.

I want approximately four visual ideas across the whole film.

Use the strongest REAL Taxtello surfaces you find in the repository.

Strong candidates include:

• Finanzcockpit / Dashboard
• Rechnungen
• Belege
• Bank / matching
• Steuergesundheit / tax overview

You do NOT need to show all of them.

Choose the visually strongest combination.

────────────────────────────────────
SUGGESTED 15-SECOND STORYBOARD
────────────────────────────────────

Treat this as a strong starting point, not a rigid template.

0.00 – 1.20

BLACK / NAVY.

A tiny warm-gold glint appears.

The glint elegantly reveals either the Taxtello mark or a fragment of the
wordmark.

No generic logo fade.

Think machined precision.

The camera moves through or past the mark and the UI begins to emerge from it.

Very little or no copy.

─────────────────

1.20 – 4.40

FINANCIAL CONTROL.

Reveal the actual Taxtello Cockpit as a dimensional product surface.

Not just a screenshot placed on screen.

Reconstruct/crop/layer it so individual interface regions can animate.

The hero financial number resolves crisply.
The chart draws in.
Supporting metrics settle slightly later.

Use subtle stagger.

A single line of copy may appear, for example:

  “Alles im Blick.”

or another equally short German phrase if you find something more fitting.

Maximum ~3–4 words.

The interface must remain recognizable as the real product.

─────────────────

4.40 – 7.50

DOCUMENT / BOOKKEEPING TRANSFORMATION.

Use a visual object from the previous scene as the transition.

Example:

A gold chart point expands into the corner of a receipt/card.
The camera follows it.
A receipt/document enters.
Taxtello identifies or organizes it.
The document snaps elegantly into its corresponding booking / financial record.

Use magnetic alignment and precision.

No cheesy scanner laser.

No floating paper tornado.

Possible micro-copy:

  “Belege. Erledigt.”

Only if it improves the scene.

─────────────────

7.50 – 10.70

MONEY / INVOICES.

Morph or transition naturally into the real Rechnungen interface.

Use one strong moment:

an invoice status changes,
a payment resolves,
an amount moves into place,
or the overview assembles itself.

Numbers should feel tactile and precise.

Use JetBrains Mono where this matches the actual product.

Gold highlights the active state.

Green is used only for a genuinely positive semantic state.

Potential copy:

  “Geld. Im Griff.”

Again: optional and extremely short.

─────────────────

10.70 – 12.80

TAX / CLARITY.

Transition into the real Taxtello tax-health / financial guidance surface.

Do not claim that Taxtello magically guarantees correct taxes.

Communicate visibility and control.

Example:

multiple noisy signals collapse into one calm, structured tax overview.

Potential copy:

  “Steuern im Blick.”

This scene should feel calmer than the previous scene.

The rhythm briefly slows.

─────────────────

12.80 – 15.00

BRAND PAYOFF.

Pull the camera outward.

The UI compresses or folds into one beautiful Taxtello product object / surface.

Darkness returns around it.

The gold Taxtello wordmark resolves.

One short brand line underneath.

Explore strong final lines such as:

  “Dein Business. Klar.”

  “Buchhaltung. Unter Kontrolle.”

  “Einfach mehr Überblick.”

  “Alles fürs Business. An einem Ort.”

Choose based on the actual product positioning you find in the repo.

Do not use a line simply because I suggested it.

The final frame must have enough stillness to register.

End confidently.

No giant bouncing CTA.

────────────────────────────────────
TRANSITIONS
────────────────────────────────────

This is one of the most important parts.

I want transitions that make the viewer think:

“Of course the next scene came from that.”

Good:

chart line → document edge
gold pill → invoice button
financial number → amount in invoice
card edge → next surface
camera push through interface element
shared geometry
mask reveal using actual product shapes

Bad:

crossfade
random wipe
spin transition
glitch
whip-pan every two seconds
generic SaaS slide-left
zoom-blur spam

Direct cuts are allowed only when a deliberate rhythmic impact benefits the film.

────────────────────────────────────
MOTION
────────────────────────────────────

Motion needs weight.

Use curves comparable to:

cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)

where appropriate.

Different elements should have subtly different arrival times.

Prefer:

anticipation
overshoot below ~2%
settling
motion continuation
shared velocity between scenes

Avoid cartoon springiness.

Camera movement should feel like a high-end macro product shoot.

Imagine we are filming a physical premium object even though it is software.

────────────────────────────────────
LIGHTING / MATERIAL
────────────────────────────────────

Use extremely subtle environmental lighting.

Possible treatments:

• soft gold rim lighting
• dark navy falloff
• faint ambient bloom
• soft specular highlight passing across a surface
• restrained vignette
• subtle grain if it materially helps

Keep the interface crisp.

Do NOT blur the product just to look cinematic.

No fake glossy reflections that destroy legibility.

────────────────────────────────────
TYPOGRAPHY
────────────────────────────────────

Use very little copy.

No sentence should compete with the product.

Headlines should generally fit on one line.

Use Plus Jakarta Sans.

Strong typography may occasionally scale very large and become a transition
device itself.

Avoid generic motion-graphics behavior where every word animates independently.

Typography should move as designed objects.

────────────────────────────────────
SOUND / RHYTHM
────────────────────────────────────

Design the motion as if it were cut to approximately 115–120 BPM:
premium, kinetic, sophisticated, not frantic.

Important moments should land musically.

Suggested sound language:

• low soft impact for major reveal
• restrained tactile UI clicks
• subtle metallic/glass tonal tick
• soft low-frequency movement during camera transitions
• elegant resolved tone at the logo payoff

Avoid:

• huge cinematic trailer boom
• EDM risers
• loud whooshes everywhere
• stock “tech interface” sounds
• rap beat
• aggressive bass

If there is no legally safe music/audio asset in the project, DO NOT pull
copyrighted audio from the internet.

Deliver the visual master without copyrighted music and create a concise cue
sheet describing where music/SFX should hit.

If suitable safe/local audio exists, use it.

────────────────────────────────────
REAL PRODUCT ONLY
────────────────────────────────────

This is critical.

Inspect current main.

Do not invent screens.

Do not invent metrics that imply real customer data.

Use clearly synthetic/demo-safe values if required.

Do not accidentally expose any personal, test-user or production information.

Reuse the visual structure of the actual Taxtello UI.

If a screen needs to be motion-separated, recreate it faithfully in React from
the real design system instead of simply scaling a giant screenshot.

The result should still look unmistakably like Taxtello.

────────────────────────────────────
IMPLEMENTATION EXPECTATIONS
────────────────────────────────────

Work directly in:

  /taxtello/beta-motion

Create the new composition alongside the existing one.

Keep existing compositions working.

Structure the new work cleanly.

Prefer reusable primitives for:

• camera surface
• product frame
• masked transitions
• text reveals
• UI region reveals
• ambient lighting
• shared-element transitions

Avoid one 1,500-line component.

Use deterministic Remotion animation driven by frame/time.

No setTimeout.
No nondeterministic animations.

Respect 60 fps throughout.

Use interpolation/spring/easing deliberately.

────────────────────────────────────
DO NOT STOP AFTER FIRST IMPLEMENTATION
────────────────────────────────────

This is a visual task.

You MUST review the actual rendered output.

Required workflow:

1. Inspect repository and real brand/product.

2. Write a concise storyboard with:
   - exact timestamps
   - key visual
   - transition logic
   - copy
   - intended emotional rhythm

3. Implement it.

4. Run typecheck / relevant checks.

5. Render representative frames at roughly:
   0.0 s
   1.0 s
   2.5 s
   4.5 s
   6.5 s
   8.5 s
   10.5 s
   12.5 s
   14.0 s
   14.8 s

6. VISUALLY INSPECT THOSE IMAGES.

Do not merely confirm that rendering succeeded.

Ask:

Does this look like an Apple-tier product film?

Does anything look like a template?

Is there too much on screen?

Is the product legible?

Are transitions logically connected?

Does Taxtello gold feel premium?

Does every frame look composed?

7. Fix visual weaknesses.

8. Render the complete film.

9. Inspect multiple exact decoded frames from the final MP4, not only browser
   screenshots.

10. Iterate again if necessary.

Do not declare success because the code compiles.

The deliverable is the FILM.

────────────────────────────────────
QUALITY BAR
────────────────────────────────────

Reject your own result if it feels like:

• a SaaS template
• a PowerPoint animation
• a website screen recording
• a generic Remotion demo
• a crypto advertisement
• an AI-generated promo template
• five screenshots sliding around
• excessive marketing copy

Every important frame should be good enough to use as a still advertisement.

I would rather have:

3 extraordinary visual moments

than

10 mediocre feature animations.

────────────────────────────────────
FINAL DELIVERABLES
────────────────────────────────────

Provide:

1. Final storyboard
2. New Remotion composition source
3. 1920×1080 / 60fps final MP4
4. Poster/final frame
5. Contact sheet with representative frames from the film
6. Exact runtime
7. List of real Taxtello assets/screens used
8. Brief explanation of the motion language
9. Any remaining visual compromises
10. Commands to reproduce the render

Save outputs in a clearly named directory such as:

  /taxtello/beta-motion/out/showreel-15/

Do not deploy anything.
Do not modify production data.
Do not merge anything.

Go all out creatively, but exercise ruthless restraint.

Make Taxtello look expensive.

title: Stop-motion paper-note animation
prompt_text:
You are my motion designer and sound designer. Build a 9.5 second vertical stop-motion "paper note" video end to end and render it to an MP4. Work in this folder. Do everything yourself: write the code, install what you need (Node, Puppeteer, ffmpeg, Python with numpy + scipy), render, look at the frames, fix problems, and give me the finished file.

MY TEXT (lines 1-3 in capitals, exactly like this):
LINE 1: [I MADE THIS]
LINE 2: [WITH AI]
LINE 3: [COMMENT "PROMPT"]
SIDE NOTE: [it's free]
SIGNATURE: [@YOURHANDLE]
The last word of line 3 is the punchline.

FORMAT
- 1080x1920 (9:16), 30 fps, 9.5 s = 285 frames. H.264 High yuv420p, CRF 18, +faststart. AAC 48 kHz stereo 320k, -14 LUFS, true peak -1.4 dBTP. Save it as out/paper_note.mp4.
- Frame 0 is already interesting: a crumpled paper ball on a painting. No fade at the end: the last 3 frames are identical and show the finished note.
- All text stays between 12 % and 78 % of the height (Instagram UI safe band).

HOW TO BUILD IT
- One HTML page with a canvas (three.js for the paper). It exposes window.V = { W: 1080, H: 1920, dur: 9.5, ready(), seek(t) }. Every visual state is a pure function of time t, so frames can render in any order. Seeded random only, never Math.random at render time.
- A Node + Puppeteer script opens the page, calls seek(frame / 30) for every frame, screenshots it and pipes the frames to ffmpeg. Max 2 parallel workers.
- The page exports its event list (time, type, x position of every letter, word, mark, doodle, tape, confetti burst). A Python script (numpy/scipy) synthesises the music and every sound effect from scratch from that list, so each sound lands on its visual frame. No downloaded samples needed.
- One command (render.sh) runs everything: scene -> audio -> frames -> MP4.

TWO CLOCKS (this is what makes it feel hand-made)
- The world runs at 12 fps stop-motion: stop k = floor(t * 12). Paper pose, unfold state, background painting and doodle loops only change on a stop, which gives the 3:2 hold cadence at 30 fps.
- The juice runs on a 24 fps sub-clock j = floor(t * 24): letter pops, ink drops, sparkles, punch-ins, mark draw-ons, confetti.
- Tempo 90 BPM: 1 beat = 8 stops = 0.667 s. Letters land on 8th and 16th notes, the LAST letter of each word lands on a beat.

BACKGROUND
- Use the painted artworks in bg/ (portrait images, cover-crop to 1080x1920). If bg/ is empty, paint 8 procedural plates in code (swirls, starry skies, engravings).
- Flip to a new plate on EVERY stop (12 times a second) in a shuffled order that never shows the same plate twice in a row. It never stops flipping, also not during the ending.
- Darken each plate to about 40-50 % (its own gain, so all plates look equally dark) with a soft vignette, so the white paper pops.

THE PAPER
- Off-white lined notebook paper (RGB about 244, 244, 240), grey-blue rules every 5.4 % of the sheet height (first rule at 9 %), a torn top edge, a torn spiral-perforation right edge and a fine fibre texture. Sheet width 0.55 of the frame, centred just above the middle.
- It unfolds in 5 states during the first second: tight crumpled ball (about 0.23 of the frame wide, big flat facets, sharp creases, rules visible on the facets) -> half-open with a standing flap -> crumpled flat-ish -> wrinkled full sheet -> flat sheet. Build it as a real folded mesh (a subdivided plane folded around hinge lines that unfolds as c goes from 1 to 0), lit by a key and a fill light with soft self-shadow. Not a 2D image swap.
- Two shadows under the sheet: a tight contact shadow and a wide soft ambient one.
- On every stop the sheet boils a little (+-0.3 deg, +-1.6 px). Each time a word finishes, re-pose it like a new photo (+-1.6 deg, +-1 % shift). Single letters never re-pose it, so the text stays readable.
- Faint hand-made detail: a pencil ghost sketch of every letter before it is inked, pencil baseline guides, an eraser smudge with crumbs, a broken coffee ring, an old fold crease, and two translucent tape strips with torn ends on the top corners (from tape/ if it has images) that slap on at 1.0 s and 1.17 s.
- SIGNATURE: write [@YOURHANDLE] in marker along the bottom edge of the paper, visible from the first flat frame to the last, so it bulges with the paper and stays readable at the end.

LETTERS
- Blue paint-marker capitals (RGB about 44, 119, 159), drawn from hand-made skeleton strokes, not a font. Each letter gets its own small wobble, rotation, size and baseline jitter, streaky ink and a faint bleed. Wide tracking. The first word of line 3 is in red marker and smaller.
- Letters appear ONE AT A TIME and pop on whole (never stroke by stroke), starting at 1.33 s. Pop on the sub-clock: frame -1 squash (1.16 x 0.60), frame 0 stretch-overshoot (1.10 x 1.24, +-4 deg), then 0.96, 1.015, rest. Anchor on the baseline. With each pop the paper dips 0.7 % and recovers, 3-5 ink droplets fly out (2 stay on the paper as dots) and 2 tiny sparkles appear.

WORD REWARDS (every finished word)

Real weight on bounces. Hard cuts on the beat. SOUND: 128 BPM electronic beat, crisp hats, sub bass. Wooden thud on each bounce, clicks per letter, a blade slice, ticks on the grid flips, a riser into the tunnel, a beat of silence, then a shatter and deep bass hit on the wordmark. No narration.

STYLE 03 — ASCII terminal:
An 8-second vertical motion graphic where everything is rendered ONLY with monospace text characters, like a 3D demo running inside a terminal. IDEA: a 3D object made entirely of ASCII characters spins inside a terminal window. Brightness maps to characters: " .:-=+*#%@". It feels like Claude Code itself is drawing. TECH: render 3D geometry yourself, sample brightness into a character grid of about 90 columns, and draw each cell as a monospace glyph. No pixels outside the glyph grid. 0-1.0s: black terminal. One monospace font throughout. MOTION: smooth 3D rotation inside a rigid character grid. Typing is linear. Glitches are 2-3 frames. SOUND: dark minimal techno around 124 BPM. Mechanical keyboard clicks for typing, a CRT hum underneath, data chirps on the glitch, a cascade of tiny ticks as the characters fall, a deep hit when "MOTION" locks. No narration.

BASE BLOCK (paste under every prompt):
FORMAT: 1080x1920 vertical, 30fps, under 10 seconds. BUILD: one self-contained HTML file. Every frame is drawn on canvas as a pure function of time (seek(t)). Stylised animated performance with real weight, clean readable poses, strong silhouettes, a micro-pause before every big reaction. PHYSICS Mass and inertia carry through every fall, glide, splash, bite and leap. @ACORN tumbles with real weight and throws a heavy splash. Water sheets off fur, spray arcs behind the sprint, bubbles rise at proper speed, reeds bend in the wake, crocodile backs sink under his weight. Nothing floats. His big tail trails half a beat behind every direction change and whips when he turns. Correct contact shadows on branch, water, scales and sand. LIGHTING Warm late-morning sun from the upper left through the canopy, visible god-rays and dappled pools on the forest floor, bright bounce off the river filling all shadows so nothing falls dark. Underwater the light turns deep green and falls in shafts from the surface. The final shore beat is lit warm and low with long soft shadows across the sand. Faint haze through the far trees. WB locked 5400K. COLOR GRADE Ginger fur glowing warm against teal-green water, the brown acorn the single solid mass in every frame it appears in, olive crocodiles blending into the reed banks, golden-yellow blossom canopy backlit by the sun, pale trunks catching rim light, white spray against dark water. Rich and saturated, no deep shadow anywhere, color tied to source and surface, not a flat list. AUDIO Full orchestral chase score with fast strings, woodwind runs and heavy comedy percussion, mixed loud. A rising violin scramble under the branch struggle, a sharp stinger as the acorn tears loose, near-silence across the slow-motion fall with only rushing wind, a huge timpani and cymbal hit on the splash, then the score racing flat out through the glide and the water run with a woodwind sting on every jaw snap and a cymbal choke on the tail bite. A warm resolving chord over the shore.

title: AI video prompt template with continuity rules and restrictions
prompt_text:
Act as a professional film director and AI video prompt engineer. I need you to help me write a detailed, production-ready AI video prompt.

Here's my idea:
IDEA: [Describe your scene in 1-2 sentences]
PURPOSE: [What emotion should the audience feel?]
MAIN CHARACTER: [Appearance, clothing, personality]
ENVIRONMENT: [Setting details, time period, lighting]

Now expand it into a production-ready prompt including:
• ACTION & MOVEMENT: Exactly what happens, the sequence of events, character acting, pacing, and timing
• CAMERA DIRECTION: Shot types (wide, close-up, over-the-shoulder, Dutch angle), camera movement (static, dolly, pan, tracking), lens choice (35mm, 50mm, 85mm), and camera angle (low, eye-level, high, bird's eye)
• LIGHTING & ATMOSPHERE: Quality of light (warm, cold, soft, harsh, directional), light sources, time of day, atmospheric effects (fog, rain, dust, lens flare)
• VISUAL STYLE: Cinematic style, color palette, contrast, film texture. Must specify a consistent look (e.g., 'Photorealistic live-action, desaturated, high contrast, grainy film stock'). Never leave the style ambiguous.

CRITICAL CONTINUITY RULES — add these to your prompt:
• CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: The main character's appearance (hair, clothing, build, face) must be identical in every shot. Lock one reference description and reuse it verbatim in each scene.
• ENVIRONMENT LOCK: Walls, floor, furniture, props, and background must not change between shots unless it's an intentional story reason.
• LIGHTING MATCH: If the scene is lit by sunset in one shot, it must be lit by sunset in the next. Time of day must not jump without a transition.
• PHYSICS & MOTION: Real-world physics. Objects don't float unless supernatural. Movements should flow smoothly without snapping or teleporting.

RESTRICTIONS — enforce these:
• No text, subtitles, logos, watermarks, or UI overlays.
• No morphing, no extra limbs, no warped faces.
• No cartoon/anime look unless that's the explicit style.
• No sudden zooms, shakes, or speed ramps unless I ask for them.

Output only the final copy-ready prompt, nothing else.

title: Clothes-rack product rail hover animation
prompt_text: Build a "clothes-rack" product rail for the product grid in this codebase. WHAT IT SHOULD FEEL LIKE - Products hang from hooks along a straight horizontal rail. At rest each product hangs SIDE-ON, showing its side photo (rest angle ~84-93deg, varied per product so the row looks real). Price tags hang from the hooks and always face the viewer. - Hover (or keyboard focus) on a product turns it to face the viewer (0 degrees) near-instantly: ~0.12s to 90%, settled by ~0.18s, no wobble. On leave it turns back to its resting angle. - The rail scrolls sideways to show more products: wheel, trackpad, touch, keyboard, prev/next buttons, mouse drag with a fling, and resting the cursor near either end (the rail runs that way). - The rail is a shallow arch, ends ~18px lower than the middle, and every hook rides it as the row scrolls. - When the rail moves, every product swings like a pendulum from the top of its hook: the hook moves first and the hem lags behind; while the rail keeps moving the hem trails at a slight lean; when the rail stops the hem swings through past vertical and settles in ~3-4s. BEFORE YOU WRITE CODE 1. Find the product grid / product card component and how product images are loaded. List the files you will change and wait for my OK. 2. Check the product images. Ideal: front, side and back shots, cut out on transparent backgrounds, on the same canvas size, with the neck on the same pixel in all three. [CHOOSE: front + side + back shots exist | front shots only (use the FRONT-ONLY FALLBACK below) | one white sample per style, tinted per colourway (use TINTING below)] 3. Do not change routing, analytics events, add-to-cart handlers, or any class name, id or data-* attribute that other code reads. STRUCTURE (adapt to the framework in use) - A scroll container (overflow-x: auto, no scroll-snap) holding a single row of product cards. The rail itself is a separate, non-scrolling bar behind the row, positioned where the hooks bend over it. - Each card stays a link to the product, with aria-label="<name>, <price>". Inside it: .hanger__swing (aria-hidden="true") swings; pivot = top of the hook hook image .hanger__spin turns; axis = through the neck .face--front front photo one plane... .face--back back photo ...rotateY(180deg) .face--side side photo crossed plane: rotateY(-90deg), photo mirrored with scaleX(-1) so the shirt's front leads .face--far side photo rotateY(90deg), not mirrored price tag after the spin, so it paints on top - CSS: - card: position: relative; fixed aspect-ratio. - .hanger__swing: position: absolute; inset: 0; transform-origin: 50% 2% (top of the hook); perspective: 640px; perspective-origin: 50% 25%. Keep it transform-style: flat. - .hanger__spin: position: absolute; inset: 0; transform-style: preserve-3d; transform-origin at the neck; transform: rotateY(var(--rest)), with --rest set per card. - faces: position: absolute, same box; backface-visibility: hidden. Front and back use opacity: var(--fw); both sides var(--sw). - side-on a product is ~40% of its card wide: overlap neighbouring cards by ~20% of their width each side; give the hovered / focused / tapped card a higher z-index. Make the card itself pointer-events: none and add a hit area the width of the hanging product (~40%), widened to the whole card while that card is turned, so overlapping cards don't steal hover and a sleeve doesn't drop it. - NEVER put filter, opacity < 1, overflow: hidden, clip-path or mask on .hanger__spin. They flatten the 3D context. Opacity, masks and drop shadows go on the faces. MOTION (plain JavaScript, one requestAnimationFrame loop, no library) - Each frame, dt = min(seconds since last frame, 0.1). Step both springs below in fixed 1/120s slices (ceil(dt * 120) substeps), so a stiff spring keeps real time on a 30fps phone and a 144Hz monitor alike. - Rail motion, read FIRST each frame (before writing any styles): speed = -(scroller.scrollLeft - lastLeft) / dt // hooks' px/s, right = + railV = 0.5 * railV + 0.5 * speed railAcc = 0.5 * railAcc + 0.5 * (railV - previous railV) / dt - Turn, per card (angle a in rad, speed w): target = (hovered and not dragging) or focus-visible or pinned ? 0 : rest w += (-900 * (a - target) - 54 * w) * dt; a += w * dt spin.style.transform = `rotateY(${a}rad)` - Crossfade, per card, from the same angle. The fades OVERLAP so at least one photo is always solid (a single 1-x fade goes see-through at 45deg): c = cos(a)^2 --fw = smoothstep(0.2, 0.5, c) --sw = 1 - smoothstep(0.5, 0.8, c) - Swing, per card (angle s in rad, speed v): v += (-30 * k * sin(s) - 2.6 * v + (0.0011 * railAcc + 0.0036 * railV) * cos(s)) * dt s = clamp(s + v * dt, -0.45, 0.45) swing.style.transform = `rotate(${s}rad)` k is per card, 0.8-1.2 (heavier products lower), so the row never swings in lockstep. Positive rotate is clockwise and carries the hem LEFT, which is what a rail moving right does, so both rail terms are added, not subtracted. - Mouse drag: on pointerdown (mouse only) remember x and scrollLeft; past 4px of movement, capture the pointer and set scrollLeft as it moves. Hovered cards do not turn while dragging. On release, keep scrolling at the last rail speed, multiplying it by exp(-4 * dt) each frame, and swallow the click that ends the drag. - Prev/next buttons: scroller.scrollBy({ left: ±60% of its width, behavior: "smooth" }). - Edge run: on pointermove (not touch), zone = min(140px, 18% of the rail's width); depth into the left/right zone d = 0..1; edgeTarget = ∓720 * d² px/s (0 outside the zones; 0 on pointerleave and while dragging). Each frame ease towards it: edgeV += (edgeTarget - edgeV) * (1 - exp(-6 * dt)) and move the rail by edgeV * dt, clamped to its ends. Keep the rail's position in a float and write it to scrollLeft (resync the float when scrollLeft moves by more than 1px for any other reason). While |edgeV| > 40, hovered cards do not turn. - Arch: draw the rail as an SVG quadratic across the visible rail, "M0 (y+sag) Q500 (y-sag) 1000 (y+sag)" with preserveAspectRatio="none" and sag = 18. Measure each card's centre (offsetLeft + width/2) once and on resize; each frame lower each card by sag * u², u = clamp((centre - scrollLeft) / railWidth * 2 - 1, -1.4, 1.4). Without JS or with reduced motion keep a straight rail and no offsets. - Start the loop on scroll, hover, focus, tap or drag; stop it when the rail is still and every card has settled (|a - target|, |w|, |s|, |v| all tiny), snapping a to target and s, v, w to 0. TINTING (if one white sample serves every colourway) - Each face: isolation: isolate; inside it a .face__tint layer (background: var(--cloth); mask: url(photo) center / contain no-repeat) and the white photo on top with mix-blend-mode: multiply. - Prepare the photo: cut out, white at true white, folds' contrast stretched a little so they survive the multiply. Solid colours only; textured or printed colourways need their own photos. FRONT-ONLY FALLBACK (if there is no side shot) - Rest at 55-65deg instead of ~90deg (a flat photo vanishes edge-on) and drop the side faces. Add 10 slices behind the front photo, spread across translateZ -11px to 11px, each a darker solid colour masked by the front photo, and a black overlay with opacity 0.35 * (1 - |cos(a)|) for shade. FALLBACKS AND ACCESSIBILITY - No JS: a CSS-only turn, scoped under a class (e.g. .rack--css) that the script removes when it takes over. Register --fw and --sw with @property (<number>, initial 0 and 1) so they transition: .hanger__spin { transition: transform 180ms cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1), --sw 80ms, --fw 80ms 60ms; } .hanger:hover .hanger__spin, .hanger:focus-visible .hanger__spin { transform: rotateY(0deg); --fw: 1; --sw: 0; transition: transform 180ms cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1), --fw 80ms, --fw 80ms 60ms; } - prefers-reduced-motion: no springs and no swing; the turn is instant. - Touch: native scroll drives the swing. [CHOOSE: a tap turns the product and a second tap opens it | a tap simply opens the product] - Keyboard: a visible :focus-visible ring; focus turns the card to face front; never block Enter from opening the product. - Animate only transform, opacity and the custom properties. No layout reads in the loop other than scrollLeft, read before any writes. DONE WHEN - At rest the products hang side-on at slightly different angles, showing their side photos; hovering one turns it to face front crisply, settled within ~0.2s, no wobble, and never see-through mid-turn. - Flinging the rail, or resting the cursor near an end, makes the hems lag behind the hooks, then swing through when it stops, then settle; tags never turn; the hooks follow the arched rail. - With JS disabled you get the CSS turn and a scrollable rail; with reduced motion, an instant turn and no swing. - No console errors; analytics and add-to-cart behave exactly as before; Largest Contentful Paint is no worse. - Finish with a summary of the files you changed and the dials to tune: turn stiffness/damping (900, 54), swing pull/damping (30, 2.6), and how hard the rail pushes the hem (0.0011 acceleration, 0.0036 speed).

title: Moon impact cinematic in Python
prompt_text: Build a 20-second 1080x1350 30fps cinematic in Python (numpy + opencv + PIL), no 3D software, CPU only. Story: the moon falls toward Earth, a steel rocket launches on an intercept, hits it, and the moon is pushed back into orbit. End frame matches the first so it loops. 1. Get the free NASA-based earth (day, night lights, clouds, specular) and moon textures from the three.js repo on GitHub. 2. Write a ray-tracer for two spheres: per-pixel ray-sphere hits, equirect texture lookup, one sun light. Earth: day/night blend with city lights on the dark side, clouds, ocean glint, blue rim plus a thin atmosphere halo. Moon: soft lunar shading with a little earthshine. 3. Stars: 9k points + a faint milky-way band, motion streaks when the camera moves fast. Scale star density with the field of view. 4. Shots: wide approach (0-3s), tracking shot behind the moon (3-6s), telephoto from low orbit with the moon over Earth's limb (6-9s), rocket launch with a glowing plume (9-11s), nose-cam rush into the moon (11-12.4s), impact (12.4s), moon recedes (12.4-17.6s), back to the opening wide shot. 5. Impact: white flash, 3-frame color inversion, camera shake, glowing crater with fissures that cool down, a shockwave ring across the surface, 3,000+ debris particles with streaks that cool from white to orange to grey. 6. HUD in a mono font: lunar distance in km (starts at 384,400), closing speed, countdown, small "render · schematic" tag. 7. Post: bloom, filmic tonemap, vignette, light grain, chromatic aberration only on the impact. 8. Sound with numpy, no melody: rumble that rises toward impact, soft clicks on 8th notes that speed up, low thumps on every cut, rocket roar, a huge low boom, half a second of near-silence, then airy breathing noise that ramps back into the opening. Low-pass at 7 kHz, -14 LUFS, true peak under -1 dB. 9. Render stills at key moments first and fix framing before the full render. Encode H.264 + AAC, faststart.
